teaser: One small head, a slope, and a huge empty sky: Goya's quietest and strangest wall.
review_notes:
Catalog year 1823 is the end of the usual date range (c. 1819-1823) for the Black Paintings.
Goya aged 77 in 1823; serious illness in late 1819; deeded the Quinta del Sordo to his grandson Mariano in September 1823; went into hiding in early 1824 and left for Bordeaux that year; died 1828: confirm details.
The Dog was on the upper floor of the house: based on later inventories and reconstructions.
Jean Laurent photographed the murals in place around 1874 before removal; claim that the photograph of The Dog shows more of the shape at right (sometimes read as a rock or cliff) should be checked.
Antonio Saura calling it 'the most beautiful picture in the world' and Joan Miro asking to see it on a late visit to the Prado: widely repeated, verify.
Dimensions about 131 x 79 cm.

lesson.text: In 1823 Francisco Goya was 77, completely deaf for thirty years, and recently back from an illness that had nearly killed him. He lived in a farmhouse across the river from Madrid with a much younger companion, Leocadia Weiss, and her children. And he had good reason to be afraid.

That year a French army marched into Spain to restore King Ferdinand VII to absolute power. Liberals, who wanted a constitution to limit the king, were jailed or executed. Many were Goya's friends. In September he signed the house over to his teenage grandson, a common way to protect property from being seized. Within months he was in hiding, and then gone to France for good.
On an upstairs wall of the house he was about to lose, he left this. The surface is about 1.3 meters high (just over 4 feet). Nine tenths of it seems to hold nothing at all.
There are only two things to visit. Begin with the one that is alive.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: A dark muzzle, one floppy ear, a single eye rolled upward. That is all we get of the dog. Its body is hidden behind the brown edge, or under it.

spots.title: The shape above
spots.text: Follow the dog's gaze up and to the right. A paler, taller form hangs in the ocher, like a cliff seen through dust or a figure that has been rubbed out. It has never been explained.

lesson.text: So what is happening? Maybe the dog is sinking in quicksand. Maybe it is swimming against a current, or simply peering over a hill at its master. Goya gave the picture no title and no story. The name “The Dog” was added by people who needed to call it something.

A photographer recorded the murals while they were still on the walls, around 1874, before they were cut out and moved to canvas. In his plate of this wall, the looming shape on the right is easier to read than it is today, which suggests part of the image faded or was lost in the move.

Whatever was lost, the proportions are Goya's own, and they are what make the picture work. Before him, an animal in a painting stood in a landscape, with trees, a horizon, a sky that looked like sky. Here the world is reduced to two flat zones and one line between them.

lines.label: The slope
lines.text: A single edge rises from left to right. Below it, dark brown. It climbs in the same direction the dog is looking, so the ground itself seems to be coming up over the animal.

lines.label: The emptiness
lines.text: From the top of the head to the top of the wall: nothing but dirty gold. This gap is the real subject. The smaller the dog, the heavier the space pressing on it.

lines.label: The look
lines.text: The eye points up and to the right, toward the pale shape. Hope, begging, fear? One raised eye carries the whole feeling of the picture.

lesson.text: The Dog shows that emptiness can be the strongest thing in a painting. Almost nothing is depicted, yet nearly everyone who sees it feels the same thing: someone small, alone, looking up.

It is hard not to read the old man into the animal: deaf, cornered, watching for a sign from above. That reading is a guess. But it explains why the picture feels less like a scene and more like a state of mind, something no painter had tried to hang on a wall before.

Modern painters adopted this wall as an ancestor. The Spanish artist Antonio Saura called it the most beautiful picture in the world and painted his own versions of the dog for decades. Joan Miró, on a late visit to the Prado, is said to have asked to see just two works: Velázquez's “Las Meninas” and this one.
Goya died in Bordeaux in 1828 without seeing the house again. The dog is still looking up. No one has ever been able to say whether anything answered.

quiz.question: How much of the dog can you see?
quiz.explanation: Just the muzzle, an ear and one eye show above the brown edge.

quiz.question: Why did Goya sign his house over to his grandson in 1823?
options: To protect it from being seized
Because the king ordered him to
quiz.explanation: With liberals being persecuted, transferring property was a way to shield it.

quiz.question: Who gave the painting its title?
options: Later people who needed a name for it
quiz.explanation: Goya left the mural without a title or a story.

quiz.question: What takes up most of the painted surface?
quiz.explanation: About nine tenths of the wall is bare, dirty gold.

facts.text: Goya left Spain for France soon after 1823 and never came back to the house.
facts.explanation: He went into hiding, moved to Bordeaux and died there in 1828.

facts.text: Goya explained in a letter that the dog is drowning in quicksand.
facts.explanation: He left no explanation; sinking, swimming or peering over a hill are all guesses.

facts.text: The ground line in the painting slopes upward from left to right.
facts.explanation: The brown edge rises in the direction of the dog's gaze.
